title: The gargantuan galaxy NGC 1132

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Thousands of ancient globular clusters swarm around the giant elliptical galaxy NGC 1132 like bees around a hive in this Hubble image, with many far more distant galaxies scattered in the background. NGC 1132 lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Eridanus.

It is probably a fossil, the remains of a huge pile-up in which galaxy after galaxy collided and merged, building a brilliant but fuzzy giant elliptical that far outshines typical galaxies. Together with the small dwarf galaxies around it, NGC 1132 is described as a fossil group, because the whole system is probably the remnant of a group of galaxies that merged in the recent past.
The globular clusters are likely survivors from the galaxies NGC 1132 has swallowed. Because they outlasted their parent galaxies, they may preserve a record of how this giant was assembled.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.90 x 3.16 arcminutes) and distance (300 million light years), the frame spans roughly 253,000 × 276,000 light-years. Its light set out about 300 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed through blue and near-infrared filters, with a synthetic green channel. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long exposures reveal faint globular clusters and distant galaxies that the eye couldn't see.
